analysis.investment_thesis: Astonea Labs fails both Magic Formula criteria decisively: an earnings yield of ~2.8% (inverse of P/E 35.6) is far below the 12% threshold, and an ROE of 0.35% implies ROIC is near zero — nowhere near the 20%+ bar. This is neither cheap nor a good business.
key_strengths: High promoter holding at 72.3% signals skin in the game
Operates in structurally growing pharma contract manufacturing
Small cap (₹165 Cr) leaves runway if execution improves
key_risks: ROE of 0.35% indicates capital is earning virtually nothing
P/E of 35.6 → earnings yield ~2.8%, deeply overvalued on Magic Formula
Near-zero institutional ownership (FII 0%, DII 0.07%) reflects no smart-money conviction
red_flags: ROE 0.35% — effectively no return on capital
Earnings yield ~2.8%, well below the 6% minimum
Newly listed (2017 incorporation) contract manufacturer with unproven unit economics
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula asks two questions: is it cheap, and is it good? Astonea fails both. At a P/E of 35.6, the earnings yield is roughly 2.8% — you'd earn more in a savings account. And with an ROE of just 0.35%, the underlying business is generating essentially zero return on shareholder capital, so ROIC is almost certainly in the low single digits at best. A contract manufacturer with commodity economics and no return on capital should trade at a discount to the market, not a 35x multiple.

There is no version of my quantitative screen where this name ranks well. The combination of premium valuation and a business earning sub-1% on equity is the opposite of what the formula seeks. I would ignore the narrative of pharma/cosmetics contract manufacturing and let the numbers speak — until ROIC migrates durably above 15% and the earnings yield expands past 10%, this is a pass.
